unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 2! In this unit you will explore celebrations and festivals from around the world, with a special focus on traditions that matter to communities across East Africa and beyond. Festivals bring people together. They remind us of our history, our values, and the things that make each culture unique. Whether it is the joy of a national independence day, the colourful lanterns of a harvest celebration, or the excitement of a local sports day, every festival has a story to tell.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Key Vocabulary section below, then study the full Vocabulary companion file.
Read the festival passage in the Reading section carefully.
Work through the Understanding questions to check your comprehension.
Study the Grammar: Prepositions for Time section and the companion Grammar file.
Complete all the Practice exercises.
Follow the Writing Workshop to write your own festival description.
Do the Listening & Speaking activities with your AI tutor or a partner.
Finish with Check Your Learning to measure your progress.

readings.title: Festivals That Bring Us Together, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every community around the world has special times when people come together to celebrate. These gatherings are called festivals, and they are woven into the rhythm of human life. Some festivals mark the changing seasons, others honour long-held customs, and still others celebrate harvests, victories, or the memory of important people. What they all share is a sense of joy, belonging, and gratitude.
In many parts of East Africa, the most eagerly awaited festival of the year is the great harvest festival, which comes at the end of the long rains. The preparations begin weeks in advance. Families clean their homes from top to bottom, market stalls fill with sacks of maize and baskets of mangoes, and tailors work late into the night because everyone wants new clothes for the celebration. Grandmothers guard their recipes like treasure, and children are sent running between houses with invitations and borrowed cooking pots.
Families rise early on the morning of the festival and put on their finest clothes. Children wear brightly coloured outfits that have been hand-stitched or newly bought for the occasion. At sunrise, people walk together to the town square, greeting neighbours with warm smiles and the words “Happy Harvest!” After the opening songs, the real feasting begins. Tables are spread with freshly made sambusas, sweet halwa, fragrant rice, and tender roasted meat. The air is filled with the rich smell of cardamom tea and the sound of laughter. Elders sit in the shade and tell stories of past celebrations, while children run through the streets, their pockets full of sweets and small gifts. On the first day, families visit relatives, and on the second day, friends gather for games and community events. It is a time of generosity: those who have more share with those who have less, and old quarrels are often reconciled.
Not every celebration is tied to the harvest. National days remind citizens of their shared history: on Independence Day, flags line the streets, bands practise for the parade, and the whole town gathers to watch the fireworks at nightfall. Schools hold festivals of their own as well. A sports day or an open day may seem small beside a national holiday, yet it teaches the same lesson: when people prepare something together, they begin to feel that they belong together.
Watch how people behave at any festival and you will notice the same qualities appearing again and again. The diligent organisers arrive first and leave last. The benevolent guests bring far more food than they could ever eat, because sharing is the point of the day. Somewhere near the gate stands a vigilant steward, quietly counting the children as they stream past. Festivals, in other words, are not only for enjoyment. They are a public performance of the values a community most wants its children to inherit.

readings.title: Festivals That Bring Us Together, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Far to the north, in the highlands of Ethiopia, the Festival of Rivers is celebrated in January. The festival marks the end of the cold season and the return of the melting streams, and it is one of the most colourful events in the Ethiopian calendar. Musicians wear magnificent, gold-embroidered robes, and they carry the Great Drum — a treasured copy of an ancient instrument — through the streets in a joyful procession. Crowds line the roads, singing folk songs and clapping. At dawn on the main day, river water is carried up and sprinkled over the cheering families. The atmosphere is both solemn and enthusiastic, a mixture of deep respect and pure celebration.
Meanwhile, in the coastal towns of Kenya and Tanzania, the Lamu Cultural Festival is held every year in the month of November to celebrate the long history of the Swahili coast. On the night before the main celebration, the narrow streets of Lamu come alive with lanterns, drums, and the sweet chanting of Swahili poetry. Men perform traditional stick dances, and women prepare elaborate, sweet-scented dishes. At noon the next day, scholars give talks about the town’s past, emphasising values such as compassion, honesty, and benevolence. Children listen attentively, and many feel inspired to be more diligent and kind in their daily lives.
Further away, other cultures greet the new year with traditions of their own. In Iran and Central Asia, families celebrate Nowruz on 21 March, the first day of spring. They clean their homes, set the table with seven symbolic items, and visit friends and relatives through thirteen days of music and feasting. In parts of Somalia, communities have historically marked the solar new year with a celebration called Dabshid. Bonfires are lit at dusk, families share outdoor meals of rice and roasted meat, and the elders recite poetry and tell stories late into the night. In the United States, harvest time brings Thanksgiving, celebrated on the fourth Thursday in November, when families gather around a long table, share an enormous meal, and take turns saying what they are grateful for. The customs differ from country to country, but the pattern is remarkably similar: fire, food, and storytelling are universal ways of drawing people together.
What makes festivals truly powerful is not the food or the decorations alone, but the way they strengthen the bonds between people. In every culture, a festival is a reminder that we belong to something larger than ourselves. The next time you attend a celebration, look around: you will see authentic traditions passed down through generations, resilience in communities that keep their customs alive, and the simple, tranquil happiness that comes from being together.

readings.title: The Hero of Kitale, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
It was early on a Monday morning in April when Imani rose before the sun. The room was still dark, and the only sound was the soft breathing of her younger brother, Kofi, asleep on a straw mat beside her bed. Their mud-brick house sat near the edge of Kitale, close to the maize farms that spread out like a green sea across the land.
Imani, now fourteen, had become known in their school as both diligent and punctual. Every teacher said the same thing: “Imani is a paragon of responsibility.” But Imani didn’t care much about praise. What she cared about was the community.
Their town had faced many problems: broken water taps, rising food prices, and a school library whose roof had fallen in during the last rainy season. Some students complained, but Imani chose to act.
Her teacher, Mr. Tariq, was a charismatic man who believed in youth leadership. One day, he announced that the school would be holding its first ever Student Leadership Election. Posters appeared around the compound with names of candidates and bright slogans.
Some candidates were loud and zealous, others charming, and one boy named Max was incredibly charismatic. Max came from a prominent family. His uncle owned the largest hardware shop in Kitale. His campaign posters were printed, not handwritten. He offered sweets to younger students and even brought a speaker to play music at lunchtime.
“Wow,” whispered Kofi as the music played. “Max is legendary.”
Imani smiled. “He may be loud, but we need a leader who is authentic.”
Imani did not have money for speakers or printed posters. What she had was a notebook, a group of close friends, and ideas. She spent her evenings creating meticulous, hand-drawn posters. They showed a tree growing from dry ground with the words: “Real leaders endure. They don’t just promise. They act.”
Her speeches were not flashy. But they were honest. “We must fix the roof,” she told the school. “We need more books. I cannot promise you music, but I promise to work.”
Imani’s words began to spread. Students whispered about how determined she seemed. Even some teachers mentioned her name in staff meetings. “That girl,” said Ms. Zara, “has the spirit of a lion. She’s so intrepid.”
On the day of the election, the school hall was filled with a clamour of voices. Max walked in first, wearing a brightly coloured, fur-lined jacket. Imani walked in later, wearing her usual neat school uniform, her braids tied back, and a quiet smile on her face.
When the votes were counted, it was close. But Imani won.
Some students cheered. Others were surprised. Max looked disappointed but shook her hand.
From that day on, Imani became a different kind of leader. She stayed late at school on Thursdays to help younger students with reading. She worked with the head teacher to organise a book drive. Her friend Jamal, who was industrious, helped carry donated books every Friday.
Imani also helped reconcile students who had quarrelled. Once, two girls fought over a missing pen. Imani sat with them under the tree near the tap and helped them talk it out. “We must be impartial,” she reminded them. “We judge by facts, not emotions.”
That same week, she helped build a small garden behind the kitchen, teaching others how to grow sukuma wiki. She asked Mr. Tariq to support them, and he agreed. Her leadership was quiet but steady.

readings.title: The Hero of Kitale, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
One day, Imani returned home late, tired but happy. Her mother looked up from the stove. “You look exhausted.”
Imani sat beside her. “We planted spinach today. Kofi helped too. He’s becoming quite agile, you know.”
Her mother laughed. “Well, that’s good. But don’t forget to rest. Even lions must sleep.”
Despite her busy days, Imani always made time for study. She was tenacious. Even when the lights failed, she lit a kerosene lamp and reviewed her notes. Her aunt once said, “Imani will be legendary one day.”
Then one Friday in June, something unexpected happened.
A teacher’s motorcycle was stolen from outside the school gate. Suspicion fell on a new student named Kian. He was quiet, often late, and didn’t have many friends. Some students shouted, “He did it!” Others said nothing.
But Imani stood in front of the class. “Let’s not rush. He is innocent until proven guilty. We must be vigilant but also fair.”
The next day, the motorcycle was found abandoned near the river. Kian had nothing to do with it. Imani had saved him from false blame.
People began to see her not just as a student leader, but as a true role model. Even the elders in town heard of her efforts. One afternoon, a woman named Mama Amara came to school to donate books.
“You must be the girl,” she said. “My grandson told me you’re the reason he wants to lead.”
Imani blushed. “I’m just doing my part.”
Over time, Imani’s name reached the local newspaper. An article was published titled: “The Benevolent Girl Who Changed Her School.” One morning, the governor of the county came to visit. He walked through the classrooms and smiled when he saw the small garden. “Who started this?” he asked.
“Imani,” several students said at once.
The governor turned to her. “You’re quite young. What inspires you?”
Imani replied, “Kindness, honesty, and hard work. I believe if we help one another, we all rise. It’s just benevolence.”
He nodded, clearly impressed. “Nice one.”
That weekend, Imani received an invitation to speak at the county youth forum. Her school bus arrived early on Saturday. She wore a clean green dress, hand-stitched by her aunt. It was modest, simple, and very much Imani.
At the forum, she spoke with confidence. Her words were enthusiastic, her manner calm and tranquil. She spoke about resilience, the need to push forward even when things are tough.
“Many people wait for a hero,” she said. “But what if you are the one? What if you can change just one thing?”
The crowd clapped, not because of music or fancy clothes, but because they believed her. Her speech was later posted online, where thousands watched and commented.
On the last day of the term, Mr. Tariq gave Imani a letter. “Scholarship application,” he said. “For a leadership camp in Nairobi. I believe you’d represent Kitale well.”
Imani stared at the form. She had never left their county.
That evening, she sat with her family under the stars. “Should I go?” she asked.
“You should,” her mother said. “Your light is not meant to stay hidden.”
Kofi, with eyes full of pride, added, “You’ll do great. And don’t forget to write!”
Imani laughed. “I won’t. But you must take care of the garden. And be punctual!”
As the bus left Kitale on Monday, Imani looked out of the window. She saw the maize farms, the school roof — now repaired — and the smiling faces of students waving goodbye. Her heart swelled, not with pride, but with hope. She didn’t want fame. She wanted change. And that, she knew, took more than speeches. It took resilience, diligence, and the courage to lead quietly.

comprehension.question: According to part 1, what are three different things that festivals can mark or celebrate?

comprehension.question: In which month is the Festival of Rivers celebrated, and what change in the land does it mark?

comprehension.question: What evidence does part 1 give that preparations for the harvest festival begin long before the day itself?

comprehension.question: Part 1 calls the harvest festival “a time of generosity”. Explain how the passage supports this claim.

comprehension.question: The writer says the customs differ “but the pattern is remarkably similar”. Using two festivals from part 2, explain what that shared pattern is.

grammar.title: Prepositions of Time: In, On and At
grammar.explanation: Prepositions of time tell your reader exactly when something happens: in holds long stretches of time, on lands on particular days and dates, and at points to precise moments.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Rule 1 — use in for longer periods. Think of in as a big container that holds a stretch of time. Months: I was born in July. Years: Kenya gained independence in 1963. Seasons: The harvest festival is held in autumn. Parts of the day: I study best in the evening. Centuries and decades: Great changes happened in the 21st century.
Rule 2 — use on for specific days and dates. Think of on as landing on a particular spot on the calendar. Days of the week: The market is busiest on Saturday. Dates: My birthday is on 15 March. Special days: We celebrate Independence Day on 12 December. Day plus part of day: The guests arrived on Friday evening.
Rule 3 — use at for precise times and fixed expressions. Think of at as pointing to an exact moment. Clock times: The ceremony begins at 10:00 AM. Specific moments: The parade sets off at dawn and the fireworks start at midnight. Meal times: Let’s talk about it at lunch. Fixed expressions: at the weekend, at night, at the moment. Festival periods: We visit relatives at harvest time, meaning during the whole festival period.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “I was born on July.” July is a month — a long period — so the container word is needed: “I was born in July.”
grammar.memoryTip: Remember I-O-A: IN holds Intervals, ON lands on Occasions, and AT points to Actual times.
grammar.practice:
Part A — write in, on or at in each gap: 1) The festival begins ______ the 20th of March. 2) We always have a big meal ______ harvest time. 3) My grandmother was born ______ 1955. 4) Classes start ______ 8:30 AM every day. 5) The school play is ______ Friday. 6) It gets very cold ______ winter. 7) The morning bell rings ______ dawn. 8) We planted trees ______ the afternoon. 9) Independence Day is celebrated ______ 1 July. 10) I finished my homework ______ the evening. 11) The lantern festival happens ______ January. 12) The family gathers for dinner ______ sunset.

=== Answer Key (Self-Check) ===
Part A: 1) on (specific date, "the 20th of March") 2) at (fixed expression naming the whole festival period, "at harvest time") 3) in (year, 1955) 4) at (clock time, 8:30 AM) 5) on (day of the week, Friday) 6) in (season, winter) 7) at (precise moment, dawn) 8) in (part of the day, the afternoon) 9) on (date, 1 July) 10) in (part of the day, the evening) 11) in (month, January) 12) at (precise moment, sunset).

grammar.title: Preposition Exceptions: Night, Next and Festival Time
grammar.explanation: A few time expressions refuse to follow the basic pattern, and these exceptions appear so often in everyday English that they are worth learning by heart.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Exception 1 — night: we say in the morning, in the afternoon and in the evening, but at night. Exception 2 — no preposition: never use in, on or at before today, tomorrow, yesterday, this, last, next or every. Say “I will see you next Monday”, not “on next Monday”, and “The market opens every morning”, not “at every morning”. Exception 3 — festival periods: “on festival morning” names one specific day, while “at harvest time” means the whole general period; both are correct, but they carry slightly different meanings.
Study these fixes: “We have a meeting in Monday” becomes “on Monday” because Monday is a specific day. “The show starts in 7 PM” becomes “at 7 PM” because 7 PM is a clock time. “I’ll see you on the evening” becomes “in the evening” because the evening is a part of the day.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “She arrives at next Friday.” Drop the preposition entirely before next: “She arrives next Friday.”
grammar.memoryTip: Say the odd pair aloud — in the morning but at night — until the exception sounds as natural as the rule.
grammar.practice:
Part A — each sentence has one preposition error; rewrite it correctly: 1) The wedding is in Saturday. 2) We celebrate the harvest festival on the end of the season. 3) She was born at 2010. 4) The bus leaves in exactly 3:00 PM. 5) The market opens at every morning. 6) I saw my friend in last Tuesday. 7) The programme starts on midnight. 8) They always travel in New Year’s Day.
Part B — write two sentences of your own: one using on with a specific festival day, and one using at with a general festival period.

=== Answer Key (Self-Check) ===
Part A: 1) "The wedding is on Saturday." (specific day) 2) "We celebrate the harvest festival at the end of the season." (fixed expression naming a point in time) 3) "She was born in 2010." (year) 4) "The bus leaves at exactly 3:00 PM." (clock time) 5) "The market opens every morning." (drop the preposition before every) 6) "I saw my friend last Tuesday." (drop the preposition before last) 7) "The programme starts at midnight." (precise moment) 8) "They always travel on New Year’s Day." (specific day).
Part B is open-ended (write your own two sentences) — self-check against the rule rather than a fixed answer: your "on" sentence should name one specific festival day (model: "We light lanterns on Eid day."), and your "at" sentence should name a general festival period (model: "We visit relatives at festival time."). Compare each against Exception 3 in the Rule and Examples above.

grammar.title: Prepositions in Action: Writing About a Festival
grammar.explanation: Knowing the rules is only half the work; confident writers weave in, on and at into full sentences and paragraphs without stopping to think.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Model paragraph: In the month of October, my family works from dawn to sunset. On the last day, we feel excited because the harvest festival is coming. At sunrise on the morning of the festival, we put on our best clothes and walk to the market square. We eat a big meal together in the afternoon.
Notice how in carries the month and the part of the day, on carries the particular days, and at pins down the exact moments. When you write your own paragraph, check every time expression against the I-O-A rule before you move on.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “The celebrations start in 9:00 AM on the morning.” Clock times take at and parts of the day take in: “The celebrations start at 9:00 AM in the morning.”
grammar.memoryTip: Before you hand work in, circle every time expression and ask: interval, occasion or actual moment?
grammar.practice:
Part A — write one sentence for each of the following, using the correct preposition of time: 1) something you do in a particular month; 2) something that happens on a specific day of the week; 3) something that starts at an exact time; 4) a festival that takes place in a particular season; 5) an event on a specific date; 6) something you do at night.
Part B — write a paragraph of five to six sentences about a festival or celebration, using in at least twice, on at least once and at at least once. Underline each preposition of time.

=== Answer Key (Self-Check) ===
Part A content is personal, so self-check the preposition category rather than exact wording — each sentence should still follow the I-O-A rule: 1) in (a month, e.g. "I visit my grandparents in December.") 2) on (a day of the week, e.g. "We clean the house on Saturdays.") 3) at (an exact time, e.g. "The parade starts at 4:00 PM.") 4) in (a season, e.g. "The harvest festival takes place in autumn.") 5) on (a specific date, e.g. "We celebrate my sister’s birthday on 3 May.") 6) at (night, e.g. "I read stories at night.")
Part B is a genuinely open-ended paragraph. Self-check using the model paragraph already given in this item’s Rule and Examples above as your pattern: confirm your paragraph uses "in" at least twice, "on" at least once and "at" at least once, and that every underlined preposition matches interval (in), occasion (on) or exact moment (at).

grammar.title: Compound Adjectives
grammar.explanation: A compound adjective joins two words with a hyphen to build one precise description, such as hand-made lanterns or a well-known singer.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Form a compound adjective by linking two words with a hyphen when the pair describes a noun that follows: gold-embroidered robes, sweet-scented dishes, hand-drawn posters, fur-lined jackets. The Hero of Kitale uses several: Imani’s hand-drawn posters, Max’s fur-lined jacket, and the hand-stitched dress her aunt made. An adverb ending in -ly is never hyphenated, even before the noun: brightly coloured outfits, freshly made sambusas. Hyphenate only when the description comes before the noun: “a well-known singer performed”, but “the singer is well known”.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “She wore a hand made dress to the festival.” When the pair sits before the noun, join it with a hyphen: “a hand-made dress”. But never hyphenate an -ly adverb: “a brightly coloured dress” is already correct.
grammar.memoryTip: Two words, one hyphen, one idea: if the pair works together as a single description, tie it together.
grammar.practice:
Part A — combine the words in brackets to form a compound adjective and rewrite the sentence: 1) She wore a ______ (sweet / scented) dress to the festival. 2) The children carried ______ (hand / made) lanterns through the streets. 3) A ______ (well / known) singer performed at the concert. 4) They served a ______ (home / baked) cake at the celebration. 5) He is a ______ (hard / working) student who helps organise school events.
Part B — find four compound adjectives in The Hero of Kitale and copy the phrase each one appears in.
Part C — write two sentences of your own using compound adjectives.

=== Answer Key (Self-Check) ===
Part A: 1) sweet-scented 2) hand-made 3) well-known 4) home-baked 5) hard-working.
Part B: real compound adjectives that appear in "The Hero of Kitale" (any four of these count as correct) — "mud-brick house" (Part 1: "Their mud-brick house sat near the edge of Kitale"); "hand-drawn posters" (Part 1: "creating meticulous, hand-drawn posters"); "fur-lined jacket" (Part 1: "wearing a brightly coloured, fur-lined jacket" — brightly coloured is adverb + adjective, so it takes no hyphen); "hand-stitched" dress (Part 2: "a clean green dress, hand-stitched by her aunt").
Part C is open-ended (write two of your own). Model: "The well-organised event ran smoothly." / "Her soft-spoken voice calmed the room." Self-check: two words joined by a hyphen, placed before the noun they describe.

grammar.title: Participle Adjectives: -ed or -ing
grammar.explanation: Participle adjectives come in pairs: the -ed form describes how someone feels, while the -ing form describes the thing that causes the feeling.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Use the -ed form for the person who has the feeling: I was amazed by the fireworks display. She felt tired after cooking all day for the feast. Use the -ing form for whatever causes the feeling: The festival was really exciting. The traditional dances were fascinating to watch. The long ceremony was boring for the little children. Test yourself by asking who feels and what causes: the children feel bored because the ceremony is boring.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “I am very exciting about the festival.” The speaker has the feeling, so the -ed form is needed: “I am very excited about the festival.”
grammar.memoryTip: Feelings end in -ed; causes end in -ing. People are usually -ed; things are usually -ing.
grammar.practice:
Part A — choose the correct form of the word in brackets: 1) The festival was really ______ (excited / exciting). 2) I was ______ (amazed / amazing) by the fireworks display. 3) The long ceremony was ______ (bored / boring) for the little children. 4) She felt ______ (tired / tiring) after cooking all day for the feast. 5) The traditional dances were ______ (fascinated / fascinating) to watch. 6) He was ______ (confused / confusing) about which day the celebration would start.
Part B — write one pair of sentences using excited and exciting correctly.

=== Answer Key (Self-Check) ===
Part A: 1) exciting 2) amazed 3) boring 4) tired 5) fascinating 6) confused.
Part B is open-ended (write your own pair of sentences). Model: "I felt excited when I heard about the trip." / "The trip was exciting." Self-check: the -ed form should describe how a person feels, and the -ing form should describe the thing causing that feeling.

grammar.title: Relative Clauses and Celebration Idioms
grammar.explanation: Relative clauses let one sentence carry extra information using who, that, where, whose or which, and idioms add the friendly, informal colour that real conversation is full of.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Join ideas with a relative pronoun: The woman who organised the festival is my neighbour. The cake that my aunt baked was delicious. Lamu is a beautiful island where a famous cultural festival is held. My friend whose poem won the competition read it aloud. The decorations, which were hand-made by the children, looked wonderful.
Now learn four idioms for talking about celebrations: catch on means to begin to understand something (“It took me a while to catch on to the rules of the game”); by the way introduces something extra (“By the way, did you hear about the festival next weekend?”); nice one praises someone (“You organised the whole event yourself? Nice one!”); hang on means wait for a short time (“Hang on a minute while I finish this lantern”).
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “The woman which organised the festival is my neighbour.” People take who or whose, not which: “the woman who organised the festival”.
grammar.memoryTip: Who for people, which for things, where for places, whose for belonging — and that can stand in for who or which in everyday speech.
grammar.practice:
Part A — join each pair of sentences using the relative pronoun in brackets: 1) The woman organised the festival. She is my neighbour. (who) 2) The cake was delicious. My aunt baked the cake. (that) 3) Lamu is a beautiful island. A famous festival is held there. (where) 4) My friend won the poetry competition. His poem was about the harvest. (whose) 5) The decorations looked wonderful. They were hand-made by the children. (which)
Part B — write a short dialogue of six to eight lines between two friends preparing for a festival, using at least two of these idioms: catch on, by the way, nice one, hang on.

=== Answer Key (Self-Check) ===
Part A (model combined sentences — wording may vary slightly; check that you kept the correct relative pronoun and the full meaning of both original sentences): 1) "The woman who organised the festival is my neighbour." 2) "The cake that my aunt baked was delicious." 3) "Lamu is a beautiful island where a famous festival is held." 4) "My friend, whose poem was about the harvest, won the poetry competition." 5) "The decorations, which were hand-made by the children, looked wonderful."
Part B is open-ended (write your own dialogue). Model: A: "Hang on, I still need to finish my lantern." B: "By the way, did you invite Mariam?" A: "Yes! Nice one for remembering." B: "I think I finally caught on to how the dance steps go." Self-check: your dialogue should use at least two of the four idioms (catch on, by the way, nice one, hang on) with their correct meanings.

writing.title: Writing 1: Describe a Festival
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Plan, draft and polish a description of a festival or celebration you have experienced or know about. Your finished piece should be at least 200 words long.
Step 1 — choose your festival: a seasonal festival such as a harvest, lantern or new year celebration; a national holiday such as Independence Day; a family celebration such as a wedding, a naming ceremony or a graduation; or a community event such as a sports day or school open day.
Step 2 — plan: note the festival’s name and when it takes place, the story behind it, the preparations people make, what happens on the day itself in order, the atmosphere, and why it matters to your community.
Step 3 — draft with this checklist: use at least three prepositions of time correctly; include at least two compound adjectives such as brightly coloured or hand-stitched; use at least one participle adjective such as excited or fascinating; include at least five vocabulary words from this unit; organise your writing into at least three clear paragraphs; and add sensory details of what you see, hear, smell and taste.
Step 4 — revise: read your draft aloud, check that every sentence begins with a capital letter and ends correctly, and make sure your description paints a picture a reader can step into.
Example opening: Every year, in the month of October, my family celebrates the harvest festival. On the morning of the festival, I wake up early and put on my new brightly coloured outfit. The house smells of freshly made sambusas and sweet cardamom tea. I feel excited and grateful because the months of hard work are finally over.
writing.modelText:
Every year, in October, our town of Kitale celebrates the harvest festival at the end of the long rains.
In the week before, families clean their homes and market stalls fill with sacks of maize. My mum sews hand-stitched decorations, and everyone is enthusiastic.
On the morning of the festival, a procession of drummers passes our gate at sunrise. The air smells of roasted maize, and I feel excited watching the brightly coloured dancers.
At night there is a feast, which we share with neighbours in gratitude. It matters because the whole community is together, and that is a tradition that endures.

items: Paragraph 1 (name, when, story behind it): Every year, in December, my family celebrates my grandmother's naming-ceremony anniversary in our home town. The tradition began generations ago when the whole clan gathered on the seventh day after a baby's birth to give thanks, and although the ceremony itself was a single day, my family later turned the anniversary into a yearly celebration of that first blessing.

Paragraph 2 (preparations, compound adjectives): In the week before the celebration, my aunts prepare mountains of sun-dried dates and freshly baked bread, while my uncle, a diligent man who never leaves a task half finished, repairs every chair in the courtyard. My cousins sew hand-stitched cushions in bright fabric, and by the morning of the event the whole compound looks brightly coloured and welcoming.

Paragraph 3 (the day itself, atmosphere, sensory detail, participle adjective): On the morning of the celebration, an elderly and charismatic storyteller arrives to retell the naming story to the youngest children, and everyone listens with fascinated attention. At midday we share a benevolent feast that no guest ever pays for, and the air smells of cardamom, roasted meat and warm bread. By evening, drummers fill the courtyard, and I feel excited every single year, even though I have heard the story many times before.

Paragraph 4 (why it matters, conclusion): This celebration matters because it keeps an authentic piece of our family's history alive, reminding every generation that a single small blessing, tenaciously remembered, can still bring an entire family together a hundred years later.

writing.title: Writing 2: Character Profile of Imani
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a character profile of Imani from The Hero of Kitale in about 100 words. Describe her personality, her actions and why she is a good leader, supporting each point with one detail from the story. Use at least five vocabulary words from this unit, such as diligent, tenacious, impartial, benevolent or authentic.
writing.modelText: Imani, the hero of Kitale, is a diligent and tenacious girl of fourteen. Her teachers call her a paragon of responsibility because she is always punctual, and even when the lights fail she studies by a kerosene lamp. She is also benevolent: she plants spinach with her brother Kofi to help families facing rising food prices. Most of all, she is impartial. When Kian, the quiet new student, was suspected of stealing a teacher's motorcycle, Imani refused to judge him without proof. She leads by working hard, staying fair and encouraging others, which is why the whole town trusts her.
writing.sentenceStarter: I would like to argue or explain...

items: Imani, the hero of Kitale, is a diligent and tenacious student who never gives up, even when the lights fail and she must study by a kerosene lamp. She proves she is a good leader through her actions: when the school library roof collapsed, she organised her classmates instead of waiting for an adult, and when Kian was wrongly suspected of stealing a motorcycle, she stayed impartial and searched for real evidence before blaming him. She is also benevolent, planting spinach with her brother to help families struggling with rising food prices. Her authentic care for fairness, rather than popularity, is exactly why the whole town of Kitale trusts her judgement.

writing.title: Writing 3: Alternative Ending in Nairobi
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine Imani arrives at the leadership camp in Nairobi. Write a continuation of the story in 150 to 200 words. Decide what she learns, who she meets and what challenge she faces, and keep her voice and values consistent with the original story. Use dialogue at least once and include at least three vocabulary words from this unit.
writing.modelText:
When Imani arrived at the leadership camp in Nairobi, the clamour of the city made her feel small. Her roommate, a charismatic girl called Amal from Mombasa, greeted her at once. "You're the one who defended the new boy," Amal said. "Everyone here has heard."
On the second day the group was told to clean a stretch of river in two hours. Some argued; others gave up. Imani listened, then quietly divided the work. "We don't need to be loud," she said. "We need to be tenacious."
By sunset the bank was clear. Imani learned that leadership in a big city was the same as in Kitale: stay diligent, stay fair, and never leave anyone behind.
writing.sentenceStarter: I would like to argue or explain...

items: When Imani arrived at the leadership camp in Nairobi, the noise of the city almost overwhelmed her after the quiet mornings of Kitale. Her roommate, a charismatic girl named Zawadi from Kisumu, introduced herself immediately. "You're the one who defended the boy nobody trusted," Zawadi said, smiling. "I read about you in the camp newsletter."

On the second morning, the camp leader gave every team just two hours to repair a broken well pump in the nearby village. Some campers argued over whose plan was best, wasting precious minutes, but Imani listened carefully to each idea before choosing. "We don't need the loudest plan," she said calmly. "We need the plan that actually works."

By sunset, clean water was flowing again, and the whole village cheered. Imani realised that leadership in a busy city camp needed the same qualities as leadership in Kitale: staying diligent when the task was hard, remaining impartial when campers disagreed, and never chasing the credit for herself.
otherAnswers: A different continuation might have Imani meet a boy who doubts girls can lead a team, and win his respect not through argument but by fixing the pump herself while he watches.
Another version could send Imani's team to rebuild a damaged classroom instead of a well, testing her patience with campers who give up much faster than she does.
Some learners might have the camp director notice Imani's fairness and ask her to mediate an argument between two older students, a much bigger responsibility than she expected.

writing.title: Writing 4: A Letter to Imani
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a letter to Imani telling her what you admired about her leadership and asking her two thoughtful questions about her experience. Open and close the letter properly, refer to at least two specific moments from the story, and explain how her example could change something in your own school.
writing.modelText:
Dear Imani,
I have just finished reading your story, and I admire how you led Kitale. When the library roof fell in, you did not wait for someone else; you organised your friends. And when Kian was accused of stealing the motorcycle, you stayed impartial and looked for the truth.
I have two questions. How did you stay tenacious when people doubted you? And were you ever afraid to speak up?
At my school in Hargeisa the playground is full of rubbish. Your example encourages me to start a clean-up group instead of complaining. Thank you for showing that quiet, diligent work changes things.
With gratitude,
Hana

When the school library roof collapsed, you did not wait for an adult to solve the problem — you organised your classmates and started clearing the damage yourselves. And when Kian was wrongly accused of stealing the teacher's motorcycle, you stayed impartial and searched for real evidence instead of joining the crowd who blamed him.

I have two questions for you. How did you stay so tenacious when some of the older students doubted a fourteen-year-old could lead anything? And were you ever afraid that being fair to Kian would make you unpopular with your friends?

At my own school, the younger students are often left out of decisions about our clubs. Your example has encouraged me to invite them to our next planning meeting instead of deciding everything without them. Thank you for showing that quiet, diligent fairness can change a whole community. With gratitude, Sagal

Others might explain that they plan to speak up for a classmate who is treated unfairly, the way Imani spoke up for Kian.

writing.title: Writing 5: Compare Two Festivals Essay
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short essay of 150 to 200 words comparing two festivals: one from the unit readings and one from your own experience. Follow a clear structure: an introduction naming both festivals, a paragraph on their similarities, a paragraph on their differences, and a conclusion saying which festival you prefer and why.
writing.modelText:
The Festival of Rivers in the Ethiopian highlands and Eid in my home town of Hargeisa are the two celebrations I want to compare.
They have a lot in common. Both begin at dawn, both bring a whole community into the streets, and both end with a generous feast shared with neighbours in gratitude.
The differences are clear. Whereas the Festival of Rivers is celebrated in January with a procession, drums and gold-embroidered robes, Eid follows a month of fasting, and its decorations are simpler: new clothes, henna and sweets for the children.
I prefer Eid, because the tradition of visiting every relative in one day makes me feel I truly belong.
writing.sentenceStarter: I would like to argue or explain...

items: Paragraph 1 (introduction naming both festivals): The Festival of Rivers described in our unit reading and Eid al-Fitr in my home town of Berbera are the two celebrations I want to compare.

Paragraph 2 (similarities): The two festivals have several things in common. Both begin very early in the morning, both bring whole neighbourhoods out into the streets together, and both end with a generous feast that families share with people who have little of their own.

Paragraph 3 (differences): The differences, however, are just as clear. Whereas the Festival of Rivers takes place in January with drummers and gold-embroidered robes, Eid follows an entire month of fasting, and its main decorations are simpler: new clothes, henna patterns and sweets for the children.

Paragraph 4 (conclusion, preference and reason): I prefer Eid, because visiting every relative in a single day, however tiring it becomes by evening, makes me feel that I truly belong to something larger than myself.
otherAnswers: A learner comparing the Festival of Rivers with a family wedding might instead prefer the wedding, because it celebrates one specific family rather than an entire town.
Another learner might prefer the Festival of Rivers itself, admiring its music and costumes even though it is not part of their own tradition.
Some learners might conclude that neither festival is 'better', arguing that both matter equally because they serve different communities in different ways.

writing.title: Writing 6: Why Festivals Matter
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose one of these questions and answer it in two well-developed paragraphs: Are traditional celebrations in danger of disappearing, and what could communities do to keep them alive? Why does food play such an important role in celebrations? Why is generosity such a common theme in festivals across the world? Support your opinion with at least one example from the unit readings and one example from your own community.
writing.modelText:
I would like to argue that generosity is a common theme in festivals because a celebration is a way of saying thank you. In the harvest festival described in our reading, families share sacks of maize and a great feast with their neighbours, and the munificent host is the one everybody praises. Giving turns a good harvest into gratitude, and gratitude into tradition.
In my own community in Mogadishu, at Eid every family cooks more than it needs so that no neighbour eats alone. The benevolence goes both ways: the giver feels proud and the receiver feels part of the ceremony. A festival without generosity would be just a day off.
writing.sentenceStarter: I would like to argue or explain...

items: I would like to argue that food plays such an important role in celebrations because sharing a meal is the clearest way people can show they belong to the same community. In the reading about the harvest festival, families cook enormous pots of food specifically so that no neighbour goes without a plate, and the smell of roasted maize becomes part of everyone's memory of the day itself.

In my own community in Kismayo, no Eid celebration feels complete without sambusas and spiced rice cooked in enormous batches and passed between houses. Food turns a celebration from something you simply watch into something you taste, smell and remember for years, which is exactly why festivals without a shared meal always feel incomplete.
otherAnswers: A learner answering the generosity question might argue instead that festivals highlight generosity because giving away something valuable, like food or gifts, is the clearest proof that a community trusts and cares for its members.
A learner answering the disappearing-traditions question might argue that celebrations survive only if young people are taught the stories behind them, not just the food and decorations.
Another learner might choose the food question but focus on a different celebration entirely, such as a wedding feast, rather than Eid.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Celebrations and Festivals" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 11-12 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'benevolent'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "Festivals That Bring Us Together, part 1" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Hero of Kitale, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Prepositions of Time: In, On and At" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.
